definitions.definition: The idea that a scientific claim must be able to be proven wrong by some possible test or observation.
definitions.example: If I say 'all swans are white,' you could falsify it by finding one black swan.

definitions.definition: Karl Popper's rule for telling science apart from non-science: a theory is scientific only if it can be falsified.
definitions.example: Astrology is not scientific by this rule because its predictions are too vague to be proven wrong.

definitions.definition: A very strict level of proof in science, meaning there is only about a 1 in 3.4 million chance the result is due to random luck.
definitions.example: When physicists discovered the Higgs boson, they required a 5-sigma standard, which is slightly less strict than 6-sigma.

definitions.definition: A system or method designed to produce knowledge reliably.
definitions.example: The scientific method is an epistemic engine because it helps us learn true things about the world.

definitions.definition: Latin phrase meaning 'faith seeking understanding' — the idea that faith leads to deeper knowledge.
definitions.example: A person might believe in God and then study theology to understand that belief better.

definitions.definition: The study of how we know things about God and religious truth.
definitions.example: Theological epistemology asks questions like 'Can we prove God exists?' or 'How do we know the Bible is true?'

definitions.definition: A method in Christian theology that uses four sources to understand truth: Scripture, tradition, reason, and experience.
definitions.example: When deciding if a new idea is correct, a theologian might check the Bible, what church leaders have said, logical arguments, and personal experiences.

definitions.definition: Repeating a process over and over, each time making small improvements based on what you learned before.
definitions.example: When writing an essay, you draft, get feedback, revise, and repeat until it's good.

definitions.definition: Getting closer and closer to a target but never quite reaching it, like a line that approaches a curve forever.
definitions.example: As you keep adding more decimal places to pi (3.14, 3.141, 3.1415...), you get closer to the exact value but never finish.

definitions.definition: A big change in the basic assumptions or way of thinking in a field of science or knowledge.
definitions.example: When people stopped believing the Earth was the center of the universe and accepted the Sun-centered model, that was a paradigm shift.

definitions.definition: The challenge of drawing a clear line between science and non-science (like pseudoscience or religion).
definitions.example: Is astrology science? The demarcation problem is about finding a rule to decide.

definitions.definition: Different theories or systems about how knowledge is gained and what counts as knowledge.
definitions.example: Science and religion have different epistemologies: one relies on experiments, the other on faith and revelation.

definitions.definition: A number in statistics that tells you how likely it is that your result happened by chance. Lower p-values mean stronger evidence.
definitions.example: If a medicine trial has a p-value of 0.01, there's only a 1% chance the improvement was random.

definitions.definition: A mapping between two things that shows they have the same structure, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system is isomorphic to the actual tracks because the connections between stations match up.

definitions.definition: Basic statements or rules that are accepted as true without proof, used as a starting point for reasoning.
definitions.example: In geometry, 'a straight line is the shortest distance between two points' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: The assumption that the laws of nature are the same everywhere and at all times.
definitions.example: We assume gravity works the same on Mars as on Earth, even though we haven't tested every spot.

definitions.definition: The idea that the universe can be understood by human reason and math.
definitions.example: Scientists assume that the laws of physics make sense and can be figured out, like a puzzle that has an answer.

definitions.definition: The philosophical and theological system of Thomas Aquinas, which combines Christian faith with the ideas of the ancient philosopher Aristotle.
definitions.example: Thomism argues that reason and faith can work together to understand God and the world.

definitions.definition: Knowledge that you have but cannot easily explain or write down, like knowing how to ride a bike.
definitions.example: A scientist might have a 'gut feeling' about which experiment to try next, based on years of experience they can't fully describe.

definitions.definition: Latin for 'Scripture alone' — the belief that the Bible is the only source of authority for Christian faith and practice.
definitions.example: A sola scriptura Christian would say that church traditions or personal feelings don't matter as much as what the Bible says.

definitions.definition: The principle that evidence from different, independent sources can converge to support the same conclusion.
definitions.example: If fossils, DNA, and geology all point to evolution, that's consilience — many lines of evidence agreeing.
